name: Ali ibn Abi Talib
role: Fourth Rashidun caliph and first Shia Imam (656-661)
summary: Ali, cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad, ruled as caliph during the first Muslim civil war. The traditions attributed to him present a government bound to the Qur'an and sunnah, equal division of public funds, care for the poor, restraint in war and personal austerity, alongside enforcement of Islamic criminal penalties. The sources hold nothing on most modern questions.

sources.title: Nahj al-Balagha (sermons, letters and sayings attributed to Ali, compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi, c. 1000), al-Islam.org translation: Letters 3, 6, 14, 24, 25, 47, 51, 53, 54, 62; Sermons 3, 40, 92; Sayings
sources.author: Ali ibn Abi Talib (attributed; compiler al-Sharif al-Radi)
sources.usedFor: His stated views on governing, justice, the poor, taxes, war conduct, consultation and his own austerity; attribution is traditional and disputed, so answers resting on it alone are low

sources.title: The Succession to Muhammad: A Study of the Early Caliphate (pp. 239-277)
sources.author: Wilferd Madelung
sources.usedFor: His record as caliph: equal division of the fay', refusal to confirm Uthman's governors, acceptance of arbitration at Siffin, the Nahrawan campaign

sources.title: Sahih Muslim, hadith 4450, 4457 and 4458 (Book of Hudud)
sources.author: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj
sources.usedFor: Ali's enforcement of the flogging penalty for drinking and his speech urging punishment for adultery

legalize-drugs.rationale: Had the drinker al-Walid flogged and counted forty stripes; alcohol is the only intoxicant on record, so the match to 'recreational drugs' is by analogy.

more-religion-public.rationale: His charters make the Qur'an and sunnah the standard for officials, judges and taxation, with religion woven through all government.

separate-church-state.rationale: Governs as caliph by religious law; in Sermon 40 he defends rule by a ruler against the Khawarij slogan 'the verdict is only God's' while holding rulers to the Qur'an.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Orders his governor Malik al-Ashtar to rule by the Qur'an and the Prophet's sunnah and to settle disputes by referring them to Allah and the Messenger.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: As caliph gave equal shares of the fay' to all entitled Muslims from his accession, over Ibn al-Abbas's objection, and refused his brother Aqil extra treasury money. Applies to Muslims; his treatment of slaves and women was unequal in law.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Letter 54 says he sought allegiance from no one until the people came to him and that it was neither forced nor bought; Letter 6 grounds the caliphate in the muhajirun and ansar's choice.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Tells Malik to set aside a share of public funds for the lowest class, orphans and the aged, and to attend to them before the powerful.

death-penalty.rationale: Will (Letter 47) orders that his killer Ibn Muljam be killed in retaliation, one blow for one blow and without mutilation.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Tells Malik to do justice even against himself and his kin, and not to say 'I should be obeyed'; rebuked a judge for a costly house.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Had some zanadiqa burnt; Ibn Abbas objected only to the method of burning, agreeing the penalty of death was proper.

elective-rulers.rationale: Letter 6 says a caliph chosen by the muhajirun and ansar is valid, but Sermon 3 and Letter 62 say the Arabs wrongly took the caliphate from the Prophet's house.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Saying 328: Allah has fixed the livelihood of the destitute in the wealth of the rich, so any hunger is the rich withholding it.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Tells Malik to appoint well-paid, tested judges and to refer unresolved cases to the Qur'an and sunnah.

premarital-sex.rationale: Delivered a speech urging that the hadd for fornication be enforced, slaves included.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Treats the Qur'an as the Book of Allah that fixes every class's rights and settles disputes, the final authority over opinion.

simple-living.rationale: Letter 45: wears two shabby garments, eats two loaves, and will not feast while others go hungry.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: Letter 14: do not fight until they begin, do not kill the fleeing or wounded, and do not harm women.

religious-offensive-war.rationale: Letter 14 forbids starting a fight; his wars were against fellow Muslims, and no offensive war for conversion is recorded.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Orders public provision for the orphans and aged who cannot work or beg, and says Allah fixed the livelihood of the destitute in the wealth of the rich.

notes: The Nahj al-Balagha was compiled about 350 years after his death and its attribution is disputed, so answers resting on it alone are low. Answers from Madelung and the hadith collections are medium. Editors' footnotes in the al-Islam.org edition are commentary and were not used. Themes searched: government and legitimacy, justice and law, economy, taxes and poor relief, war conduct, religion and the state, crime and punishment, women, slavery. His Sermons on women and the Nahj sayings disparaging women were read but do not state a legal position, so gender statements are null. Silence on modern institutions is left null.
